citation.title: Confirmation bias in AI-assisted decision-making: AI triage recommendations congruent with expert judgments increase psychologist trust and recommendation acceptance
citation.venue: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 2(1), 100066

reading.source_scope_note: Human responses to mock clinical chatbot interfaces, not diagnostic outputs generated by a tested AI or measured patient outcomes. Prior clinical bias studies cited by the article were not independently read here.
access_limits: All 15 extracted pages read, including repository cover, methods, result tables, discussion, limitations and references. Figure 2 on PDF page 8 was rendered and visually inspected; other figures were interpreted through captions and text, not independently digitized.
Linked supplementary vignettes, prompts, questionnaires, analysis code/data and researcher explanations for textual inconsistencies were not obtained.

study.profession: 92 students and 22 practitioners/trainees/counsellors/nurses, including two practicing clinical psychologists
study.design: Between-subject randomized congruent versus incongruent recommendation across three vignettes; outcomes averaged within person
study.outcomes: Stated likelihood of incorporating recommendations and perceived trustworthiness; expertise measured by self-report before the task

summary: Congruent mock recommendations produced higher mean intended acceptance and trust than incongruent recommendations. Both measures covaried strongly, and measured self-rated expertise moderated congruence effects. The vignettes had no uniquely correct diagnosis, so congruence-related preference is consistent with confirmation bias but does not demonstrate actual diagnostic error, unbiased counterevidence rejection or superiority of one final diagnosis.

findings.term: Confirmation bias includes selective interpretation and weighting
findings.definition: Information matching an initial belief can receive greater trust and weight than conflicting information; in this clinical-vignette study, congruent AI advice was rated more favorably.
findings.previous_definition: Reaching a positive conclusion without stating and testing the alternative explanation.
findings.revised_definition: Seeking, interpreting or weighting information to favor an existing belief while neglecting relevant alternatives or disconfirming evidence.
findings.definition_revision_reason: The old wording described one audit symptom rather than the broader established construct. The source explicitly defines confirmatory information seeking, distortion and weighting, which can apply to positive or negative beliefs.
findings.novelty_rationale: The concept already exists. Congruence-driven trust, selective adherence and biased artificing are retained as related descriptions/applications, not separate synonyms counted as new behaviours.

findings.evidence_scope: Random assignment to mock recommendation congruence changed self-reported acceptance and trust in 114 eligible participants, mostly students. The authors could not test diagnostic accuracy because all recommendations were designed to be plausible.
findings.boundary: Agreement is not automatically biased: initial knowledge can legitimately justify rejecting contradictory advice. Demonstrating a congruence preference does not establish objectively worse diagnosis or uniquely identify a motivated cognitive mechanism. Cherry-picking is the narrower practice of selecting supportive evidence from material already gathered.

findings.term: Congruence effects and automation reliance are not mutually exclusive
findings.definition: The study found selective trust in advice matching initial diagnoses, which qualifies a blanket-acceptance account but does not show that automation bias is absent.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds an outcome distinction within existing confirmation and automation entries rather than create a new hybrid bias.
findings.evidence_scope: No human-adviser comparison, no clearly correct/incorrect advice manipulation and no actual diagnostic-action outcome. A congruence effect can coexist with other forms of overreliance.
findings.boundary: Do not infer immunity to automation bias from a lower incongruent acceptance rating. This design cannot establish calibrated checking, correction of known AI errors, an actual reduction in bias, or patient safety.

methodological_limits: The sample was predominantly students; the article’s umbrella term psychologists must not be mistaken for 114 practicing clinicians.
Intended acceptance and perceived trust are self-report outcomes, not observed final diagnosis changes, error detection or patient benefit.
Vignettes were generated with ChatGPT-4 and validated as plausible by clinicians; the MindAssist recommendations themselves were fixed mock interfaces, not an evaluated deployed chatbot.
No unique diagnostic ground truth or correct-versus-incorrect advice manipulation; the authors explicitly acknowledge this constraint.
Self-rated expertise was measured, not randomized or equivalent to years of professional experience. Its moderation does not prove that expertise causes bias.
Trust and acceptance were correlated, so their causal direction or a mediating effect cannot be inferred from the correlation alone.
The article reports Type I error=.5 in its power analysis, which may be a typographical error; do not silently replace it with .05 or treat the power calculation as independently verified.
One acceptance question with six response options is described as a six-item Likert scale; this is not evidence of six independent acceptance items.
Covariate human-versus-AI preference was assessed after the vignette intervention; covariate-adjusted estimates do not remove all possible confounding or post-treatment conditioning concerns.

Some prose repeats congruent where incongruent is intended and mixes outcome names in the moderator discussion; Tables 5 and 6 are used to distinguish acceptance from trust, without silently rewriting the article.

Selection/exclusions, missing outcome responses, three scenarios and nonrandom recruitment limit generalization. The listed exclusions and partially retained respondents are not assumed to imply a completely balanced sample.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Kücking measures agreement with advice known to be wrong, while this study deliberately has no unique correct diagnosis. These outcomes cannot support identical accuracy or bias-mitigation claims.

The review distinguishes prior beliefs, selective reliance and feedback. The current congruence manipulation supplies a bounded short-session example, not a universal inability of experts to learn appropriate reliance.

deferred.term: Biased artificing; selective adherence to matching AI advice
deferred.reason: These are descriptions of confirmation-compatible selection already covered by the existing entry. The cited SLB primary sources were not independently read here.

deferred.term: Self-perceived expertise causes overclaiming or diagnostic error
deferred.reason: Expertise was self-reported, impossible-knowledge claims were not tested, and diagnosis accuracy was not established. The Atir primary source is a lead, not a read empirical result.

limitations: No new standalone entry added; confirmation bias receives a source-grounded definition correction and both entries gain bounded evidence.
No clinical deployment, therapeutic recommendation or benchmark outcome is changed.
